setupSteps: Bar height (gym or home): the bar should be high enough that you hang with straight arms and your feet clear of the floor, and low enough to reach safely from a box. One buying guide suggests standing reach plus about 8 inches (20 cm) as a target; another list notes ceiling-mounted bars need roughly 9 ft (2.7 m) of finished ceiling for good head clearance. These are vendor guidance, not a standard; no authoritative height rule was found.
Head clearance: your head must clear the ceiling and any light or fan at the top of the rep, with the chin above the bar. If it does not, use the lat pulldown (Gym 25) instead.
Dismount space: keep the area under and around the bar free of benches, weights and sharp edges; one guide suggests a non-slip mat on slick floors. No landing-zone dimensions were found.
Bar check: shake the bar before use; it should not wobble. Tell staff if it is loose, bent or the fixings look worn.

Doorway bars at home: use only a bar rated for your body weight (most listed ratings are about 100-135 kg, one review site, est.), fitted to a solid frame as the maker instructs, and check it every time. Do not kip or add weight on a doorway bar. If you cannot be sure the frame is sound, do not use it.
Use a box or bench for height: step up so the bar is at about forehead height and place your hands; do not jump up and swing from the floor as a beginner.

Hand placement: grip the bar with a full, closed grip (thumbs wrapped), hands about shoulder-width apart, palms away for a pull-up. One beginner guide says shoulder-width is enough, and another says slightly wider; wider grips shorten the range (ExRx notes range is compromised if the grip is too wide).
Take your feet off slowly, bending the knees, or keep one foot on the box for the first sets; ask staff or a partner to stand nearby the first time.
Keep thumbs wrapped (thumbless grips slip more easily; coach-level advice).
Lower under control to straight arms, then lower your feet to the box or floor; bend the knees on landing. Do not drop from a high hang with straight legs, and do not let go at the top.
If you cannot finish a rep: lower slowly to a hang, then step down; do not let go mid-air.
Pull-up (overhand): FitPlate start for the dead hang and scapular pull-up; ACE says a narrow overhand grip moves some load from the lats toward the upper back muscles.

Chin-up (underhand, about shoulder-width): usually easier for beginners because the biceps help more; use it if you can already do a few controlled negatives. Many sources agree it loads the biceps more.

Neutral grip (palms facing, on parallel handles): often friendlier on the wrists and shoulders (coach-level; one forum report of an elbow-tendon sufferer switching to neutral); FitPlate offers it as a variation for people with elbow or shoulder discomfort.

steps.title: Step up and take the bar
steps.action: Stand on a box, take the bar with both hands, overhand, about shoulder-width, thumbs wrapped.
steps.feel: Firm grip; light stretch in the armpits.
steps.visualCheck: Front: hands level and even on the bar. Side: bar slightly in front of the face, not behind the head.

steps.title: Take your feet off, into a hang (Dead hang, A)
steps.action: Bend the knees and lift the feet slowly; hang with arms straight (not locked hard) and the body still.
steps.feel: Stretch in the shoulders, forearms working.
steps.breathing: Breathe normally; never hold your breath.
steps.visualCheck: Front: no twisting; side: body hangs straight under the bar.

steps.title: Set the shoulders (active hang)
steps.action: Gently draw the shoulder blades down away from the ears without bending the elbows. Some coaches prefer a fully relaxed passive hang first for a few weeks, so the passive hang is allowed as a regression.
steps.feel: Shoulders move away from the ears; body rises 1-2 cm.
steps.breathing: Breathe out as the blades move.
steps.visualCheck: Front: neck looks longer; elbows still straight.

steps.title: Scapular pull-up (B)
steps.action: From the hang, pull the shoulder blades down, pause 1 second, then let them rise slowly back to the dead hang.
steps.feel: Muscles under the shoulder blades and lats switch on.
steps.breathing: Out on the pull, in on the lowering.
steps.visualCheck: Side: only a small rise, elbows straight.

steps.title: Pull the chest up (strict rep or assisted rep)
steps.action: After the shoulder blades move, bend the elbows and pull the chest toward the bar, elbows down and back, trunk still.
steps.feel: Lats and upper back; biceps help.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbows move down, not out to the side; side: no kick and no swinging.

steps.title: Chin above the bar
steps.action: Reach the top with the chin clearly above the bar; keep the neck neutral (do not crane the head).
steps.visualCheck: Front or side: nose above the bar line; body still.

steps.title: Controlled lowering (also Negative pull-up, C)
steps.action: Lower slowly all the way to straight arms. For a negative, start at the top (stepped up from a box) and lower for 3-5 seconds (est.; coaches suggest 5-7 s for stronger beginners).
steps.feel: Back and arms working as they lengthen.
steps.visualCheck: Side: no dropping; elbows straight at the bottom.

steps.title: Finish and step down
steps.action: At the last rep, hang with straight arms, find the box with your feet, then let go.
steps.visualCheck: Feet on the box or floor before the hands release.

commonMistakes.title: Kipping or swinging
commonMistakes.text: Kipping or swinging. Why: it adds momentum, loads the shoulders and elbows in uncontrolled ways, and hides weak strength; most coaching sources say beginners should build 5-10 strict reps first (blogs; the specific research cited in blogs was not verified). Fix: start from a still hang, no leg drive, use negatives and bands instead.

commonMistakes.title: Half reps (no full hang, or the chin not above the bar)
commonMistakes.text: Half reps (no full hang, or the chin not above the bar). Why: limits strength gains and range. Fix: start each rep from straight arms and finish with the chin above the bar; use a band or the assisted machine (Gym 27) to complete the range.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping fast from the top
commonMistakes.text: Dropping fast from the top. Why: the shoulders and elbows take a sudden stretch. Fix: lower for 3-5 seconds.

commonMistakes.title: Grip too wide
commonMistakes.text: Grip too wide. Why: the range shortens and the shoulder gets stressed (ExRx notes the range is compromised). Fix: shoulder-width grip.

commonMistakes.title: Shrugging into the ears or craning the neck
commonMistakes.text: Shrugging into the ears or craning the neck. Why: the neck and upper trapezius take over. Fix: shoulder blades down first; neck long.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling with the arms only (curling up)
commonMistakes.text: Pulling with the arms only (curling up). Why: the back stays quiet, the biceps and elbows tire. Fix: set the shoulder blades, then drive the elbows down.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: raises blood pressure briefly. Fix: breathe out on the pull.

commonMistakes.title: Jumping off the bar or letting go at the top
commonMistakes.text: Jumping off the bar or letting go at the top. Why: risk of ankle and knee injury and a hard landing. Fix: lower to straight arms and place the feet on the box or floor.

commonMistakes.title: Using a loose or unrated bar
commonMistakes.text: Using a loose or unrated bar. Why: the bar can slip or the doorframe can fail. Fix: shake test; follow the maker's rating.

commonMistakes.title: Using only bands to progress
commonMistakes.text: Using only bands to progress. Why: bands help most at the bottom and fade near the top, so strength at the top may lag. Fix: add negatives and thinner bands over time.

safetyNotes: Shoulder problems: the full hang loads the shoulder with traction; people with a rotator cuff tear or impingement should avoid or modify it until a physiotherapist approves. Hanging-focused sites advise a physician or physiotherapist check first and warn that a fresh tear needs rest and assessment; sharp, catching or electric pain is a stop signal (several sources on unfamiliar domains; weighed lightly).

Elbow tendon pain (golfer's elbow or tennis elbow): grip-heavy pulling, especially an overhand grip, often aggravates it; reduce the load or use a neutral grip, or pause pull-ups, and see a professional (Penn Medicine for the condition; weaker blog sources for the exercise link).
Lower back pain: do not arch or swing; ask a professional.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis, heart disease: see the table.
Spotter: not needed for dead hangs or scapular pull-ups. For negatives and assisted pull-ups, ask staff or a partner to stay near the first time and have a box under your feet.
Equipment check: shake the bar, check the band for cracks, wipe chalk and sweat; bands can snap back, so hold the band when removing the foot.
Gym etiquette: wipe the bar, do not hog the rig between sets, do not film other members and ask staff before filming.

Note: all sources for this item were seen only as search-result summaries (pages not opened in full); many are coaching blogs. The 160/90 degree elbow thresholds, the 150 degree hip limit, nose-above-bar top rule, the 3 s minimum rep, the 15-30 s hang and 3-5 s negative durations, and all sets, reps and rest values are FitPlate choices (est.), not validated. Not found: a professional-body prescription for dead hang, scapular pull-up or negative duration; an authoritative bar-height or landing-space standard; a verified doorway-bar weight standard; peer-reviewed support for the kipping-injury claims quoted in blogs; condition-specific sources for knee pain, lower back pain, obesity, PCOS and shoulder problems; Harvard Health and Mayo Clinic pages on pull-ups; the primary ACOG page on hanging exercises; full text of Dickie et al. 2017.

conditionCautions.change: After clearance: assisted or machine versions at a light load, continuous breathing, no straining
